newsitem.title: RUSSIA: FEATURE - Russia confidence may turn investment outflow tide.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Russia confidence may turn investment outflow tide.

text.p: Russians who have sucked money out of their weak economy for years are finally putting some back in, joining foreigners who may have felt like guinea pig investors.

Russian net international reserves grew strongly between January and May, indicating that capital flight, which saw Russians taking out about 10 times as much money as foreigners invested directly last year, is slowing or ending.

Industry desperately needs funds to rebuild the tattered economy, which has shrunk every year since the fall of communism in 1991, but Russians have sent money abroad or converted it into dollars and hidden it for years, keeping interest rates high and promises of recovery unfulfilled.

"This is the first time we have seen this positive dynamic since mid-1995 and it's positive evidence to suggest capital flight is at least slowing and may have reached the time when it turns," said Renaissance Capital chief economist Roland Nash.
"This is exactly the kind of evidence we have been looking for."

Net Russian international reserves more than doubled in April to $4.2 billion at the beginning of May, officials at the Central Bank say, adding that the bank has bought dollars and sold roubles since February to meet demand for the domestic currency.
EVIDENCE THAT CAPITAL LEAK PLUGGED IS TENTATIVE
Evidence Russians are ready to keep money at home is still tentative and some economists still see tens of billions of dollars fleeing the economy abroad or into hiding in Russia this year.

"In the last five years, at least $100 billion has flowed out of the country," says Khalid Sheikh, ABN-Amro senior economist for Central and Eastern Europe, who predicted 1997 capital flight would slow to a maximum of $20 billion.
Estimates by many leading economists that capital flight was $20 billion last year were conservative, Sheikh said. "This is a realistic $20 billion."

Economists hope Russians who have been robbing the economy of funds by keeping their savings at home in dollars -- there are more dollars in Russia than roubles, by most estimates -- will put their money in the bank.
Russian Economic Trends economist Al Breach said more than $8.7 billion had been converted to dollars in 1996, but the trend could reverse this year.
"Stabilisation has to be hard to get people to save in roubles -- this is the bit after stabilisation. What you would suspect is happening now is 'Ivan' is not saving in dollars."
Foreign investors and organisations have partially made up for the domestic outflow, with the International Monetary Fund putting up $10 billion over three years.
But foreigners are still concerned.
"The worry is -- why are Westerners putting money in if the Russians who know what is going on here are taking money out," Breach said.

Deutche Morgan Grenfell put 1996 capital flight at $20-$30 billion, versus foreign net direct investment of $2.2 billion and estimated portfolio investment, which soared in the fourth quarter after the T-bill market was opened to foreigners, at $8 billion.
BIG TAX DEBTORS PAYING UP -- THIS TIME

Major industrial tax debtors, under pressure from the reformist government appointed three months ago, are paying billions of dollars in back taxes owed for years, creating a one-off major boost for the rouble and stemming capital flight.
The natural gas monopoly Gazprom's search for roubles to pay taxes has helped strengthen the rouble for weeks, traders say.
Government officials have said Gazprom has already paid about $400 million and will pay all federal government debts, put at about $2.6 billion, by the end of June.
But Russia is still struggling with tax reform and parliamentary leaders say a new tax code intended to simplify the system and improve collection may not be passed by next year.
Many exporters keep profits abroad in part to avoid huge taxes and the current crackdown may not be able to maintain its momentum.
"The tax system is relatively difficult to enforce," Nash said.
DOUBTS THAT INDUSTRY WILL GET NEEDED CAPITAL
Industry, which needs investment most, may not get much soon.

Portfolio investment in government and corporate securities attracts most interest from foreigners and the government says bank interest rates, at 30-60 percent, are still too high for industry to borrow.
Officials hope T-bill rates, about the bank rate for good corporate borrowers, will be down to 20 percent by year end.

Breach predicted that most foreign funds would continue to flow into securities while major infrastructure changes needed to make the business environment more friendly for direct investment were made.

"Having your money in securities is not so bad, but having your money in direct investment is a high cost business, in the sense of the administrative costs of setting up a business," he said. "The business environment is not completely friendly."

Nash said Russia would have to make sure inflation, which it has brought down to less than 20 percent from more than 2,000 percent a few years ago, did not rise again as roubles poured into the economy.
But Russia's cash-poor economy, flooded with IOUs since cash roubles to pay debts are scarce, has a lot of room for roubles sold by the Central Bank, Breach said.
"There is so much room for money to take over and not be chasing the same goods, it can't spark inflation," he said. "This is only good news."
